stances.claim: The dismal drug-case prosecution record across past governments is structurally explained by police failure to observe constitutionally-mandated arrest and evidence-gathering procedures -- and the consequent application of the fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree doctrine, which makes illegally obtained evidence inadmissible even when it tends to prove guilt.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-explanation framing (low conviction rate = procedural defect, not judicial leniency)

stances.claim: The arrest MUST precede the search -- the process cannot be reversed, and evidence obtained in an unlawful search cannot justify a post-facto arrest of the suspect; this temporal-ordering rule is non-negotiable and explains why even shabu seized from a suspect's body can become inadmissible if the procedural sequence is violated.
stances.rhetorical_move: temporal-ordering rule emphasis (sequence as legal absolute)

stances.claim: The Sindac decision establishes that 'reliable information alone -- even if it was the product of well-executed surveillance operations -- is not sufficient to justify a warrantless arrest' because surveillance-derived information does not constitute the personal knowledge of the arresting officer that the warrantless-arrest exceptions require.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-quotation deployment to establish bright-line rule

stances.claim: The Manago decision establishes that when post-incident investigation yields sufficient information to enable warrant procurement, the failure to obtain a warrant before searching/arresting taints the evidence -- the constitutional warrant requirement is the default, and warrantless exceptions are construed strictly against the police.
stances.rhetorical_move: default-vs-exception framing (warrant is default, exceptions narrow)

stances.claim: The remedy to the dismal conviction record is not to weaken constitutional protections but for the police to study meticulously and follow strictly the constitutional process -- improving conviction rates by upgrading police procedural compliance, not by undermining the protections themselves.
stances.rhetorical_move: moral-lesson framing prescribing institutional self-improvement over rights-relaxation

notable_anecdotes: The vivid hot-pursuit example: 'the officer sees the victim fall from a bullet wound without seeing who actually pulled the trigger; yet, he personally sees the suspect running away from the origin of the shot while holding a smoking gun' -- using cinematic specificity to make the personal-knowledge requirement concrete.

The Sindac Q&A: surveillance-based arrest with shabu found in bodily search → 'Reliable information alone -- even if it was the product of well-executed surveillance operations -- is not sufficient to justify a warrantless arrest' → acquittal. The most pedagogically structured single-case treatment in CJ's drug-procedure columns.

The Manago Q&A: officer witnesses robbery but loses fleeing suspect, traces him next day via investigation, intercepts car and finds shabu → search-before-lawful-arrest renders evidence tainted → acquittal. Pairs with Sindac as a 'two ways to fail' demonstration.
The 'fruit of the poisonous tree' metaphor preserved verbatim -- the central rhetorical anchor of the entire column, doing more analytical work than any technical phrasing could.
The closing 'Moral lesson' single-sentence prescription -- pedagogically structured close that mirrors the Q&A format and tells police exactly what to do without dressing it up.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the dismal drug-case conviction record of past governments to police failure to observe constitutionally-mandated arrest and evidence-gathering procedures, citing two recent Supreme Court decisions both penned by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe: Sindac v People (Oct 3, 2016) and People v Manago (Aug 17, 2016), both producing acquittals under the fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree doctrine. Typically the drug evidence is shabu or marijuana seized after a search of the suspect's body, effects, vehicle, or home -- but under the Constitution, searches require warrants based on probable cause, with the narrow exception of a search incident to a lawful arrest (arrest MUST precede search; the sequence cannot be reversed, and evidence from an unlawful search cannot justify a post-facto arrest). Warrantless arrests are limited to three Rules-of-Court exceptions: (1) in flagrante delicto -- the suspect's overt act done within the officer's view (officer sees the actual shooting); (2) hot pursuit -- offense just committed plus officer's personal knowledge of facts (officer sees the victim fall and the suspect fleeing with a smoking gun); and (3) escaped prisoner. CJ applies the doctrine through Q&A: in Sindac, an arrest based on reliable surveillance information producing a shabu seizure was held unlawful because 'reliable information alone -- even if it was the product of well-executed surveillance operations -- is not sufficient to justify a warrantless arrest' since the officer lacked personal knowledge; in Manago, an officer who witnessed a robbery but lost the fleeing suspect and traced him next day via investigation could have secured a warrant -- and his pre-arrest vehicle search tainted the shabu evidence. CJ closes with the moral lesson: to improve the conviction rate, the police should study meticulously and follow strictly the constitutional process -- strengthening compliance rather than weakening protections.
